extracted.intended_audience: general readers and people interested in corporate PR, marketing students/professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Identify common failures and best/worst practices in corporate crisis communication and marketing by examining real-world PR disasters and their aftermaths. The page is a listicle of case studies illustrating what companies did right or wrong in public messaging, product launches, recalls, contests, and stakeholder relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis aftermath handling
rubrics_metrics.description: “the way the team handles the aftermath can make or break them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle the aftermath decisively and well; poor or lacklustre responses can magnify damage. Anti-patterns: avoidance of press conferences, stonewalling, slow uncoordinated messaging (example: Boeing’s initially lacklustre response after the door-plug incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperate with investigations and be '100% transparent' about the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond quickly and honestly to incidents, but coordinate with investigative/legal constraints. Examples: praised transparency (ideal) vs. Boeing being sanctioned for sharing non-public investigative information (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take responsibility — avoid blame‑shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept accountability rather than blaming partners or customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Own mistakes promptly; throwing partners under the bus (e.g., Boeing blaming Alaska Airlines) damages credibility and fuels criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy and sensitivity in messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empathetic, appropriately‑toned public statements, not self‑centered or tone‑deaf remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid statements that make the crisis about executives (example: BP CEO saying 'I would like my life back'). Good messaging centers victims/customers and acknowledges harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid victim‑blaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute fault to victims of disasters or tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blaming victims (example: The Sun’s post‑Hillsborough coverage) is a severe reputational error and can cause long‑term boycotts or loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product safety must trump cost‑cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise safety in product design and supply decisions instead of saving small amounts of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: eliminating safety features to save costs (example: Ford Pinto omission of a fuel-tank liner). Such decisions lead to catastrophic PR and legal fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt recalls and decisive safety action
rubrics_metrics.description: When consumer safety is at risk, act quickly (recall/halt production) to protect customers and restore trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: Johnson & Johnson’s immediate nationwide Tylenol halt and recall rebuilt trust. Delay or denial is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive or intrusive technical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not deploy hidden, invasive, or deceptive technology on customers' devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: installing covert software (example: Sony’s CDs installing a rootkit) — leads to strong backlash and legal problems. Be transparent about security/DRM and get consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet user‑generated naming/contest mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Design contests/online polls to avoid abuse, trolling, and offensive outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipatterns: fully open anonymous naming/voting (examples: Mountain Dew naming contest or similar 'Boaty McBoatface' outcomes). Use moderation, curated options, rate limits, and safeguards against mass‑gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing and cultural sensitivity of campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid campaigns that are tone‑deaf to current events or cultural contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of bad timing: Malaysia Airlines' 'My Ultimate Bucket List' after MH370/MH17, McAfrika burger during famines. Ensure cultural and temporal sensitivity checks before launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing content on users
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not impose unwanted content on customers' devices or accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: unexpected distribution of content (example: Apple pushing U2 album onto users' libraries) — leads to anger even if intent was promotional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful customer service and complaint handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat customers fairly; avoid punitive or heavy‑handed responses to complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failures: Bank of America having a customer arrested for asking about a check; dealerships forging paperwork. Good practice: transparent, helpful service that protects consumer rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect customer data and security
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure robust data security and communicate promptly if breaches occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: slow/no disclosure of data leaks (example: Lime Crime's alleged data breach and lack of early communication) — causes loss of trust and regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exploiting tragedies for profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not appear to monetise or opportunistically market during or immediately after tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: sending sale emails/discounts after a terrorist attack (Åhlens) or insensitive promotional tie‑ins. If engaging, prioritize community support and empathy, not sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough risk assessment for promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess worst‑case outcomes and unintended consequences before promotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: McDonald’s Olympic promotion miscalculated outcomes and lost money; Pepsi Philippines prize error sparked violence. Plan for edge cases and ensure contract/legal safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sexist, offensive, or exclusionary advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure ads do not demean, sexualise unduly, or alienate large customer groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: overtly sexist ads (Carl’s Jr.), campaigns perceived as promoting sexual aggression (Bud Light perceived messaging). Use diverse review panels and sensitivity testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and accurate product communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe what a product is and how it differs from others in plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure example: Wii U advertising left consumers unsure whether it was an add‑on or a new console. Avoid ambiguous messaging that confuses buyers and retailers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow legal and investigatory protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect rules in official investigations and legal processes; do not disclose prohibited information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boeing was sanctioned by the NTSB for sharing investigative info contrary to party agreements. Coordinate statements with legal counsel and investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee and supplier treatment matters for reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: How a company treats employees, customers, and suppliers affects public perception and recovery potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert opinion: changing mindset about treating employees/customers/suppliers is fundamental to turnaround (example: advice for Boeing recovery). Poor supplier/employee relations (cost-cutting, layoffs) can fuel crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aggressive legal retaliation against critics/customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from suing or criminalising customers or small critics as a first response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: suing a customer over a complaint (Tan Hiep Phat/energy drink fly case) can generate huge community backlash and loss of goodwill. Prefer transparent dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional learning and systemic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from prior incidents and implement systemic change rather than surface-level fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of repeat mistakes (example: Boeing failing to learn from 2018/2019 crashes) shows the need for real organizational reform. Demonstrable policy/process changes rebuild trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offensive imagery or insensitive naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that marketing names, imagery and hashtags cannot be easily misread or offensively reinterpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Susan Boyle hashtag fail, products named close to tragic events (AYDS/AIDS confusion), Kool‑Aid vs Flavor‑Aid confusion after Jonestown. Pre‑screen creative assets broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet stunts for public safety and legal risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure guerrilla marketing/stunts do not create public safety scares or legal issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: Adult Swim LED street signs near bridges caused bomb scares and backlash. Coordinate with local authorities and legal teams for public activations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincere, specific apologies and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologies should be genuine, acknowledge harm, and include specific corrective steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good example: Johnson & Johnson’s decisive actions helped rebuild trust. Insincere or vague apologies (or none at all) prolong damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate launches with stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate product release timing to retailers, developers, and partners before public announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: surprising partners/retailers with an early release (example: Sega Saturn), which damages retail/publisher relationships and consumer confidence. Align PR and supply chain timelines.
